newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: HASHIMOTO ARRIVES IN SYDNEY
Japan's Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto has arrived in Sydney at the beginning of a two day visit to Australia, his first since assuming office.
Mr Hashimoto is now travelling to a Sydney hotel after his flight from the United States.
He will be delivering a speech at a function in Canberra this evening, where he's expected to outline his view of Australia's role in the Asia/Pacific region.
PORT ARTHUR VICTIMS REMEMBERED IN THREE MAJOR CEREMONIES
In Tasmania, the main memorial ceremony for today's anniversary of the Port Arthur massacre will be held at the historical site's convict church.
Thirty-five candles will be lit in memory of those who were killed one-year-ago by 28 year-old gunman, Martin Bryant.
As well, a metre-long ceremonial candle will be lit, with the names of the victims engraved on its stand.
The ceremonial candle will be taken to Hobart for an evening service at St David's Anglican Cathedral.
Later in the night, the Roman Catholic Archbishop of Hobart will celebrate a special mass at St Mary's Cathedral.
CHANCE OF WA UNION BLOCKADE BEING CANCELLED UNLIKELY
WA's Trades and Labour Council says the only thing that will stop tomorrow's state-wide industrial action is a guarantee from the Premier to withdraw the new industrial legislation in its entirety.
The union blockade begins at midnight tonight and is likely to cut Western Australia off from the rest of the country.
Thousands of workers are preparing for the 24-hour strike, which will disrupt industry, hospitals, schools, transport, and flights in and out of Perth.
Yesterday, Premier Richard Court made another appeal for the action to be called off, saying amendments to the labour laws will be detailed in the Legislative Council tomorrow.

But it appears unlikely there'll be any change to the Bill's main provisions with the Government's refusal to back down on some parts such as donations to political parties and union access to workplaces.
SHIPPING REPORT DUE OUT THIS WEEK
Australia's coastline will be thrown open to international competition if the Federal Government accepts a proposal by the Shipping Reform Group.
The Group's report recommends the abolition of cabotage - a regime that protects Australian registered ships from competition from foreign owned vessels.
The Government's expected to release a report on the proposal this week.
A move to open up the coastline would be in-line with the
Government's pre-election commitment to tackle high shipping costs.
The Transport minister's office has rejected opposition to the plan from the Maritime Union, which warns it would lead to so-called "ships of shame" plying Australian waters.
CALLS FOR FREEZING OF BILLION DOLLAR FUND REJECTED
Calls by farmers to put a freeze on the A$1.4 billion Indigenous Land Fund have been rejected by a Victorian Barrister.
Bryan Keon Cohen says the Federation doesn't know what it's talking about.
The fund was established to assist Aboriginal groups seeking native title, and the NFF says the Wik decision means the fund should be used to compensate native title claimants.
Mr Keon Cohen says nothing's changed in relation to what the fund was established for.
He says it hasn't got anything to do with compensating Aboriginal people for native title that's been extinguished.
LAWYER SAYS COASTAL MANAGERS SHOULD TAKE NOTE OF INQUEST

Coastal management authorities around the nation have been warned to pay close attention to an inquest into the deaths of nine people in a rockfall on a West Australian beach last year. Five adults and four children died last September at Gracetown, south of Perth, when a limestone cliff they were sheltering under to watch a school surfing carnival collapsed.
Perth lawyer, John Quigley, who's representing the families of the victims, says there's evidence local authorities were aware of the dangers.
SUBMISSIONS TO BE HEARD TODAY ON WORK FOR THE DOLE LAWS
The federal government's "Work for the Dole" legislation will come under scrutiny in Sydney today when a Senate committee hears submissions from welfare organisations, youth groups and the ACTU.
The Australian Council of Social Service will reject the scheme and call on the government to implement a program of voluntary work.
ACOSS also wants the government to reconsider cuts to labour market programs.
FULL-TIME CARETAKER FOR DINOSAUR FOOTPRINTS
The Environment Minister has announced a plan to further protect fossilised dinosaur footprints at a site in Western Queensland.
Brian Littleproud says his department and the Winton Shire Council will jointly provide a full-time caretaker at the Lark Quarry footprints site.
He says his department will spend nearly A$100,000 to ensure protection.
